title: Asthma: Confirm Variable Airflow, Then Step Therapy to Control and Risk
bottomLine: Asthma is a variable airway disease that should be supported by objective evidence when feasible. Assess both current control and future exacerbation risk, ensure inhaled-corticosteroid-containing therapy when asthma is confirmed, and step treatment only after checking diagnosis, inhaler technique, adherence, triggers and comorbidity.
recognize: Variable wheeze, dyspnea, chest tightness and cough that change over time or with triggers support asthma.
A patient can have few daily symptoms but still carry high exacerbation risk from prior severe attacks, poor adherence or high reliever use.
differentiate: COPD, vocal-cord dysfunction, heart failure, bronchiectasis, reflux and anxiety can mimic asthma symptoms.
Normal spirometry between episodes does not exclude asthma; objective variability may require repeat testing or another validated pathway.
assessment: Assess symptom frequency, nocturnal symptoms, activity limitation, reliever use, exacerbations, ED/hospital history, smoking/vaping, allergens/occupational triggers and comorbidity.
Observe inhaler technique and assess adherence/access before escalating therapy.
workup: Use spirometry with bronchodilator response or other accepted objective evidence of variable airflow limitation when possible.
Use peak-flow monitoring, bronchoprovocation or specialist testing when diagnosis remains uncertain.
management: Use an inhaled-corticosteroid-containing regimen appropriate to age/severity and current CTS guidance; avoid LABA monotherapy in asthma.
Provide a written action plan, trigger reduction, vaccination and smoking/vaping cessation support.
Step up or down based on sustained control/risk after confirming diagnosis and treatment use.
medicationSafety: High reliever use suggests poor control/risk and should trigger reassessment rather than simply more refills.
Systemic corticosteroids carry cumulative metabolic, bone, ocular and infection toxicity; frequent bursts are a signal for regimen review/specialist care.
redFlags: Poor response to initial bronchodilator therapy
counselling: Teach inhaler/spacer technique and the action plan, including when to seek urgent care rather than repeatedly self-treating at home.
followUp: Reassess after exacerbations and treatment changes; consider specialist referral for severe/refractory disease, diagnostic uncertainty or repeated systemic-steroid need.
examTrap: Escalating asthma medication without checking inhaler technique/adherence—or using LABA monotherapy in a patient with asthma.
oneLinePearl: Asthma treatment starts with proof of variability and succeeds only when technique, adherence and risk are managed together.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society 2021 Asthma Guideline — current

title: COPD: Confirm Persistent Obstruction, Then Treat Symptoms and Exacerbation Risk
bottomLine: COPD requires compatible exposure/history plus persistent post-bronchodilator airflow obstruction; symptoms alone are insufficient. Treatment is built from smoking/exposure reduction, vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation/activity and inhaled pharmacotherapy matched to symptoms and exacerbation risk, while asthma features change the anti-inflammatory strategy.
recognize: Progressive exertional dyspnea, chronic cough/sputum and recurrent exacerbations in a person with tobacco, biomass or occupational exposure are typical clues.
Exacerbations are acute worsening beyond daily variation and may be triggered by infection or other cardiopulmonary events.
differentiate: Asthma can coexist and changes therapy because an ICS-containing strategy is needed when asthma is truly present.
Heart failure, bronchiectasis, PE and deconditioning can mimic or compound COPD symptoms.
assessment: Assess exposure history, dyspnea/function, exacerbation/hospitalization history, sputum, oxygenation, weight/frailty, inhaler technique and comorbid cardiac disease.
Check alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency risk/testing indications according to current CTS guidance.
workup: Confirm persistent obstruction with quality spirometry and classify symptom/exacerbation burden.
Use imaging, blood gas or additional testing when symptoms are disproportionate, complication is suspected or diagnosis is uncertain.
management: Use long-acting bronchodilator therapy according to current CTS stable-COPD guidance and symptom/exacerbation burden.
Add anti-inflammatory therapy selectively based on asthma features/exacerbation phenotype rather than giving ICS to every patient.
Prioritize smoking cessation, vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation and exacerbation action planning.
medicationSafety: ICS can increase pneumonia/thrush/bruising risk and should have a clear indication.
Oxygen is prescribed for hypoxemia under validated criteria, not for dyspnea with normal oxygenation.
counselling: Teach inhaler technique, smoking cessation and when exacerbation symptoms require urgent assessment.
followUp: Track symptoms, exacerbations, technique/adherence and oxygen need; reassess diagnosis if decline is faster than expected.
examTrap: Diagnosing COPD from chronic cough alone without spirometry—or giving chronic oxygen simply because the patient is breathless.
oneLinePearl: COPD is persistent obstruction plus exposure context; treatment targets symptoms, exacerbations and function.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society 2023 Stable COPD Pharmacotherapy Guideline — current

title: Pneumonia: Confirm the Syndrome, Judge Severity, Match the Setting
bottomLine: Pneumonia management begins with confirming a compatible lower-respiratory syndrome and deciding severity/disposition. Community- and healthcare/hospital-associated exposures change likely organisms and empiric therapy; use local guidance and microbiology rather than applying one antibiotic regimen to every infiltrate.
recognize: Cough, dyspnea, pleuritic pain, fever, tachypnea, hypoxemia and focal chest findings support pneumonia, but older/immunocompromised patients may present atypically.
An imaging infiltrate without a compatible clinical syndrome can represent edema, atelectasis, aspiration injury, hemorrhage or other disease.
differentiate: Acute bronchitis usually lacks focal consolidation/hypoxemia/systemic severity and does not benefit from routine antibiotics.
Aspiration pneumonitis, PE and heart failure can mimic pneumonia and require different treatment.
assessment: Assess oxygenation, respiratory rate/work, BP, mental status, hydration, frailty, comorbidity, aspiration risk, recent hospital/antibiotic exposure and immune status.
Use a validated severity tool only as an adjunct to clinical judgment and social/functional disposition factors.
workup: Use chest imaging when pneumonia probability is meaningful; obtain microbiology when severe disease, resistant-organism risk or treatment failure makes results actionable.
Avoid indiscriminate cultures in uncomplicated low-risk outpatient pneumonia.
management: Select empiric therapy from setting, severity, comorbidity, resistance risk, allergies and current local/Canadian guidance; reassess and narrow/adjust when data return.
Provide supportive care, manage hypoxemia/sepsis and treat source/complications.
Hospitalize when instability, hypoxemia, severe frailty, inability to take therapy or other high-risk features make outpatient care unsafe.
medicationSafety: Antibiotic duration should be evidence-based and response-linked rather than automatically prolonged.
Review renal/hepatic function, QT risk, C. difficile risk and interactions when choosing therapy.
counselling: Explain expected recovery and specific return precautions; do not equate sputum colour with antibiotic need.
followUp: Reassess lack of improvement, recurrent focal pneumonia or persistent imaging/symptoms for alternate diagnosis or complication.
examTrap: Treating an imaging opacity as pneumonia without a compatible syndrome—or choosing outpatient therapy despite hypoxemia/instability.
oneLinePearl: Pneumonia is syndrome + imaging + severity; the setting and host decide the regimen.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada respiratory antimicrobial stewardship

title: Pulmonary Embolism: Pretest Probability, Imaging, Then Hemodynamic Risk
bottomLine: PE diagnosis should follow pretest probability rather than reflex D-dimer or CT. Once confirmed, distinguish hemodynamic instability/high-risk PE from stable disease because disposition, thrombolysis/intervention and anticoagulation strategy depend on physiologic risk and bleeding context.
recognize: Acute dyspnea, pleuritic pain, hemoptysis, syncope, unexplained tachycardia/hypoxemia or DVT signs can indicate PE.
A normal oxygen saturation or absence of leg swelling does not exclude PE.
differentiate: Use a validated pretest-probability approach to decide whether D-dimer can rule out disease or imaging is needed.
Troponin/BNP/RV strain are risk markers after/around diagnosis; they are not stand-alone PE diagnostic tests.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics first, then VTE risk factors, bleeding risk, pregnancy, cancer, renal function and prior anticoagulation.
Look for shock, syncope, RV strain and significant hypoxemia that change urgency.
workup: Use D-dimer only where pretest probability makes it useful; use CT pulmonary angiography or an appropriate alternative based on probability, pregnancy/renal/contrast context.
Ultrasound can support diagnosis when DVT is found and chest imaging is problematic in selected cases.
management: Start anticoagulation when confirmed/highly suspected and bleeding risk permits according to the acute pathway.
High-risk PE with shock/hypotension requires immediate specialist/emergency reperfusion consideration rather than routine outpatient anticoagulation.
Stable low-risk PE may qualify for outpatient treatment only when clinical and social safety criteria are met.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant choice/dose depends on renal function, pregnancy, cancer, interactions and bleeding risk.
Thrombolysis has major bleeding risk and is reserved for appropriate high-risk contexts rather than all RV strain/troponin elevation.
counselling: Teach anticoagulant adherence/bleeding precautions and urgent return for worsening dyspnea, syncope or bleeding.
followUp: Clarify treatment duration/provoking factors and reassess persistent dyspnea for chronic thromboembolic disease/post-PE complications.
examTrap: Ordering D-dimer in a clearly high-probability unstable patient—or thrombolysing every PE with a positive troponin despite stable hemodynamics.
oneLinePearl: PE reasoning has two probabilities: probability of disease, then probability of deterioration.
sourceBasis: Thrombosis Canada pulmonary embolism clinical guide

title: Pleural Effusion: Transudate, Exudate, Infection, Malignancy, or Blood?
bottomLine: Pleural effusion is a sign with a broad differential. Decide whether the cause is already clinically clear and responding, or whether diagnostic thoracentesis is needed; when fluid is sampled, interpret protein/LDH plus pH/glucose/cell count/microbiology/cytology according to the clinical question.
recognize: Dyspnea, pleuritic discomfort, decreased breath sounds and dullness can occur, but small effusions may be incidental.
Heart failure commonly causes bilateral transudative effusions; infection, malignancy, PE and inflammatory disease commonly produce exudative patterns.
differentiate: An uncomplicated CHF effusion improving with diuresis is different from a unilateral, febrile, loculated or nonresolving effusion.
Empyema/complicated parapneumonic effusion requires drainage/source control rather than antibiotics alone.
assessment: Assess size, laterality, symptoms, fever, cancer/VTE risk, cardiac/renal/hepatic disease, anticoagulation and response to therapy.
Use bedside ultrasound/imaging to characterize free versus loculated fluid when intervention is considered.
workup: Perform diagnostic thoracentesis when the cause is uncertain and the result will change management.
Interpret fluid with serum comparison and cause-directed microbiology/cytology; no single fluid marker should be interpreted outside the syndrome.
management: Treat the underlying condition and drain infected, large symptomatic or otherwise indicated effusions using the appropriate procedural/specialty pathway.
Refer recurrent malignant, loculated or unexplained effusions for specialist management.
medicationSafety: Do not give repeated empiric antibiotics for an undiagnosed effusion without evaluating infection/source-control need.
Anticoagulation management around procedures is individualized rather than one universal hold rule.
counselling: Explain whether thoracentesis is diagnostic, therapeutic or both and who owns pending cytology/culture results.
followUp: Close the loop on fluid studies and repeat imaging only when clinically indicated; persistent/recurrent unexplained fluid requires definitive diagnosis.
examTrap: Automatically tapping every bilateral CHF effusion—or treating a complicated parapneumonic effusion with antibiotics alone despite drainage criteria.
oneLinePearl: Pleural fluid is sampled to answer a question; the syndrome tells you which question matters.

title: Hemoptysis: Stabilize the Airway, Localize the Source, Find the Cause
bottomLine: Hemoptysis severity is defined by airway/hemodynamic threat as much as volume. First distinguish true lower-respiratory bleeding from nose/GI sources, stabilize major bleeding, then evaluate infection, malignancy, bronchiectasis, PE, vascular lesions and anticoagulation-related contributors.
recognize: Blood mixed with sputum/cough supports respiratory origin; hematemesis and posterior epistaxis can mimic it.
Small recurrent hemoptysis in a high-risk smoker or patient with bronchiectasis/TB still requires diagnostic evaluation.
differentiate: Massive/life-threatening hemoptysis is an airway emergency because asphyxiation can occur before exsanguination.
Anticoagulants can worsen bleeding but should not be assumed to be the sole cause without looking for underlying pathology.
assessment: Assess airway, oxygenation, hemodynamics, estimated volume/rate, side if known, anticoagulants, cancer/TB/bronchiectasis/VTE risk and infectious symptoms.
Look for oral/nasal/GI sources and signs of anemia or coagulopathy.
workup: Use CBC/coagulation/renal testing and chest imaging according to severity; CT/CTA and bronchoscopy are chosen based on stability and suspected source.
Investigate TB promptly when epidemiology/symptoms fit and institute airborne precautions when respiratory TB is being evaluated in healthcare settings.
management: Life-threatening bleeding requires airway protection, resuscitation, reversal of major coagulopathy when appropriate and urgent bronchoscopy/interventional radiology/thoracic expertise.
Stable small-volume hemoptysis still requires cause-directed evaluation rather than automatic antibiotics.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant/antiplatelet interruption or reversal depends on bleeding severity/thrombotic risk and requires a deliberate plan.
Avoid NSAIDs or other bleeding-risk drugs when clinically significant active bleeding is present unless specifically indicated.
counselling: Give explicit emergency instructions for increasing bleeding, dyspnea, dizziness/syncope or chest pain.
followUp: Ensure CT/bronchoscopy/culture/cytology results are closed-loop and recurrent unexplained bleeding reaches specialist assessment.
examTrap: Calling hemoptysis 'from the anticoagulant' without investigating malignancy, infection or bronchiectasis—or focusing on millilitres while airway status worsens.
oneLinePearl: In hemoptysis, airway threat defines danger and the anticoagulant is a contributor, not automatically the diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Canadian Tuberculosis Standards where TB is suspected

title: Tuberculosis: Infection, Disease, Airborne Precautions, and Public Health
bottomLine: Separate TB infection from active TB disease. New respiratory/systemic symptoms or abnormal imaging in a person at risk require disease evaluation before preventive therapy; suspected respiratory TB in a healthcare setting requires prompt airborne precautions, microbiologic diagnosis and public-health coordination.
recognize: Risk is higher with exposure to active TB, birth/residence in high-incidence regions, HIV/immune suppression, selected congregate settings and certain Indigenous/community contexts shaped by structural inequities.
Active pulmonary TB may cause persistent cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis or abnormal imaging, but presentations vary.
differentiate: TST/IGRA support TB infection; they do not by themselves distinguish latent infection from active disease.
A positive infection test should not trigger preventive treatment until active TB disease is reasonably excluded.
assessment: Assess symptoms, exposure/contact history, country/community epidemiology, immune status, prior TB/testing/treatment, pregnancy, medications and liver disease.
Use culturally safe, non-stigmatizing history and consider barriers to follow-up/medication access.
workup: For suspected respiratory TB, obtain appropriate respiratory specimens for molecular/microbiologic testing and chest imaging according to Canadian TB Standards.
Use TST or IGRA for infection testing in appropriate populations/indications; interpret results by immune status and exposure risk.
management: Initiate airborne precautions immediately in healthcare settings when respiratory TB is suspected/evaluated and coordinate public health.
Active TB treatment is multidrug and program/specialist guided with susceptibility information and adherence support.
Preventive treatment uses a recommended Canadian regimen only after active disease is excluded and interaction/hepatotoxicity risks are reviewed.
medicationSafety: Rifamycins have major drug interactions; isoniazid/rifamycins and other agents require hepatotoxicity monitoring based on regimen and patient risk.
Do not start single-drug 'latent TB' therapy in a patient with symptoms or imaging concerning for active TB.
redFlags: Respiratory TB with hypoxemia or severe disease
Pregnancy/major immunosuppression with suspected active disease
counselling: Explain the difference between infection and disease, why preventive treatment matters, and why public-health contact follow-up is part of care rather than punishment.
Address stigma, housing, transportation, language and medication-access barriers explicitly.
followUp: Close the loop on cultures/susceptibilities and public-health actions; monitor regimen adherence/toxicity and completion.
examTrap: Starting latent-TB treatment after a positive IGRA without checking symptoms/chest evaluation for active disease—or failing to institute airborne precautions for suspected respiratory TB.
oneLinePearl: Positive TB infection test? First exclude disease; suspected respiratory disease? Airborne precautions and microbiology now.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada TB resources
